question: NDM-1 (New Delhi Metallo-β-lactamase) resistance genes spread rapidly between different bacterial species in hospital settings primarily through:

answers.text: Conjugation — plasmid transfer via sex pilus between bacteria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. NDM-1 genes are carried on mobile genetic elements (plasmids, transposons, integrons) that transfer between bacteria via conjugation — direct cell-to-cell contact through a sex pilus. This horizontal gene transfer explains why NDM-1 appears simultaneously in Klebsiella, E. coli, Acinetobacter, and other species.

Transduction involves bacteriophages packaging bacterial DNA and transferring it between cells. While it occurs in nature, phages have limited DNA-carrying capacity and are far less efficient than conjugation for transferring large multi-resistance gene cassettes like those encoding NDM-1.

answers.text: Transformation — uptake of naked DNA from the environment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Transformation requires natural competence — the ability to take up free DNA from surroundings. Most clinically important Gram-negative pathogens are not naturally competent, and the hospital environment degrades free DNA rapidly. Conjugative plasmid transfer is far more efficient.

answers.text: Spontaneous point mutation in chromosomal β-lactamase genes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NDM-1 is an acquired metallo-β-lactamase gene, not a mutation of an existing chromosomal gene. It resides on transferable plasmids that spread between species via conjugation — this horizontal acquisition is far more rapid than de novo chromosomal mutation.

overallFeedback.feedback: NDM-1 is carried on mobile plasmids and spreads between bacterial species via conjugation — direct cell-to-cell contact through pili. This horizontal gene transfer, not mutation, explains the rapid cross-species dissemination of carbapenem resistance.
Conjugation via mobile genetic elements (plasmids carrying NDM-1, integrons, transposons) is the dominant mechanism for inter-species spread of carbapenemase resistance in hospital settings.
